s01.text: When you empty your trash bin, you assume the file is instantly erased from your solid-state drive.

s02.text: In truth, your operating system never erases data from flash memory: it only removes the file entry from the file system table.

s03.text: NAND flash has a physical constraint: it can write data in sixteen kilobyte pages, but it can only erase in massive four megabyte blocks.

s04.text: Because flash cells cannot be overwritten, saving one new file forces the drive to read, erase, and rewrite an entire multi-megabyte block.

s05.text: Without help, this read-modify-write cycle creates massive write amplification, slashing SSD write speeds by up to eighty percent.

s06.text: To prevent this, the storage industry created the TRIM command, telling the SSD controller which blocks are dead the moment you delete a file.

s07.text: TRIM lets the drive controller erase dead flash blocks in the background, keeping write speeds high and preventing premature drive failure.
